prompt: How do GameCube/Wii decompilation projects build one whole-program type model (struct layouts, field types, pointer vs integer, function prototypes) shared across translation units, inferred from how the binary uses each value (load/store widths and offsets, call arguments, vtables), and how do they keep m2c output (which types unknown values as s32/long or ?) consistent across TUs: m2c --context, ctx.h generation, Ghidra/IDA type export, dtk symbols, and which errors (pointer expected, not a struct/union, illegal operands void*+int) disappear with a shared context? For every claim give the primary source (repo file, issue, PR, compiler manual) and state it as a falsifiable prediction: 'with X, mwcc emits Y; with X', it emits Y''. Mark anything unverified.

query: What do GameCube and Wii decompilation repositories actually contain in their shared headers and context files, and how often do matching functions still fail to compile because the types were guessed wrong from the binary?
Why do some functions in a decompilation project stay unmatched even after the struct layouts and types look correct, and what causes the remaining byte-level differences in the compiled output?
At what point does a shared, centrally maintained type model start slowing contributors down or causing regressions, for example when a struct fix breaks functions that had already matched?

Why does the decompiler's output keep guessing plain integers for values that are really pointers or structs, and what has to be known about each value for a type to be chosen consistently in every source file?

What measured error rates do decompilation projects and published studies report for pointer-versus-integer and struct-versus-scalar type decisions when each function or source file is analysed in isolation, and who measured them?

At what point does supplying more type information, such as struct definitions, function prototypes and symbol sizes, stop removing compiler errors and start introducing new mismatches in the generated code?

What happens to compile errors and to byte-for-byte matching when the shared type definitions are wrong, incomplete or contradict each other across source files, and at what point does a shared model make things worse than per-file guesses?

What happens to a reconstructed program when one shared struct definition has the wrong field width or padding, and how do those errors show up as compiler output differences rather than compile errors?
At what point does sharing one type definition across all files in a reconstructed codebase start causing more mismatches than it fixes, and what do the failures look like?

Do decompilation projects for other consoles or other compilers, such as those for the N64, PS2 or GBA, build and maintain their shared type model differently, and would their methods work for GameCube and Wii code built with the Metrowerks compiler?

What happens to a matching decompilation project when types exported automatically from a reverse-engineering database are compiled with an old Metrowerks compiler, and which constructs in those generated headers cause the compiled output to stop matching the original?

Why do some decompilation projects that share type definitions across several game versions or titles end up forking or copying their headers instead of keeping one shared source, and what went wrong for them?

learning: [DERIVED][MEDIUM] The Dolphin SDK is statically linked into every GameCube and Wii game, so once its functions are matched the remaining unmatched work in a new game is mostly game-specific code. The community already runs separate SDK decompilations for the 2001 and 2004 versions, which implies version-specific shared code is a recognised unit of reuse, though the sources give no measure of how much time it saves. — Capacidad: You can stop assuming that matching a game's shared SDK code is a one-off cost per title, and instead plan on a reusable base that makes each later game cheaper to decompile. — Evidencia: S3 states the SDK is linked into every game and that matched SDK code makes new games easier; S2 lists dolsdk2001 and dolsdk2004 as separate repositories; no savings figure is given. — Ledger: C1 (S2, S3)

[DERIVED][MEDIUM] Matching depends on reproducing the exact CodeWarrior compiler version and flags used originally, and a flag mismatch makes every function unmatchable. Compiler versions across titles range from 1.0 to 1.7, so a project that has not pinned its toolchain will produce failures that look like wrong type guesses but are really toolchain errors. — Capacidad: You can judge a decompilation effort's reliability by whether the exact compiler version and flags are pinned, rather than by how clever the person or AI doing the matching is. — Evidencia: S3 says CodeWarrior codegen is version-specific, that a flag mismatch makes every function unmatchable, and that versions range from 1.0 through 1.7; the attribution of failures to toolchain rather than types is my inference. — Ledger: C2 (S3)

[DERIVED][LOW] The contents converge on one dividing line: centralize decisions that affect multiple teams (shared handoffs, controls, reporting, completion definitions) and leave local what stays within one team's work. A shared baseline with bounded local additions avoids both a central bottleneck and silent erosion of standards, which is the same risk as one fix breaking pieces others already rely on. — Capacidad: You can decide which shared rules stay under one owner and which teams may change on their own, using whether a change's consequences reach beyond a single team as the test. — Evidencia: S8 and S10 independently give the same rule for when to centralize versus decentralize, based on cross-team impact and cost of variation. — Ledger: C7 (S8, S10)

[DERIVED][LOW] Three distinct symptoms point to three different fixes: repeated waits for routine approval means streamline review; the same exception requested again and again means formalize a permitted local option; and handoff problems from inconsistent local changes mean tighten the shared boundary. Tracking queue length for shared teams is proposed as a standing health measure. — Capacidad: You can spot that a shared model has become a drag by watching for specific symptoms, and respond differently to each, instead of reacting to a vague feeling that the process is slow. — Evidencia: S8's FAQ lists the three friction patterns and matching adjustments, and S10 proposes dependency health (queue length for shared teams) as a metric; neither gives a threshold number. — Ledger: C8 (S8, S10)

[HYPOTHESIS][LOW] When a central specialist team (the example is UX) does all work for every feature team, queues grow and it becomes a bottleneck. The proposed alternative is for the central team to maintain reusable patterns, coach other teams, and join temporarily only on novel work, with autonomy measured as the share of work delivered without its direct help. — Capacidad: You can stop expecting a central team to do all the work for everyone and instead fund it to teach and productize reusable patterns, so its queue does not become the bottleneck. — Evidencia: S10 offers this as a single practitioner's model with a worked example and no measured outcomes. — Ledger: C9 (S10)

[DERIVED][MEDIUM] A flag mismatch makes every function unmatchable and looks like a source-code problem, so a stalled project may be a configuration problem rather than a talent or effort problem. Checking the build against one already-matched function is the cheap diagnostic before blaming the people or the code. — Capacidad: You can stop treating a project's compiler flags as a minor setup detail and recognize that a wrong flag setting makes every function look unfixable, so effort should be spent verifying the build settings before judging team progress. — Evidencia: S39 states that a flag mismatch makes every function unmatchable and looks like a source problem, and that the same C with different flags produces different bytes; it does not address auto-exported type headers specifically. — Ledger: C31 (S39)

[OBSERVED][MEDIUM] A project can reach 90 percent function coverage and still fail to rebuild the final ROM because of data layout, literal pools, or one stubborn function. For GameCube and Wii work with Metrowerks CodeWarrior, matching is harder than on N64 because C++ code generation is less predictable, so the 'linked' milestone is the honest completion measure. — Capacidad: You can stop reading a high function-coverage figure as proof that a decompilation project is nearly finished, and ask instead whether the whole build links to identical bytes. — Evidencia: S39 gives the 90 percent coverage example and defines 'linked' as the strongest result, and notes Metrowerks C++ codegen is less predictable than N64 output. — Ledger: C32 (S39)
